title: Chapter 66 – The Cloud Road
html:
[Lin Clan – Lin Jian]

They leave on the third day of the fourth month, at the hour before the sun clears the east wall, and no one cries.

It is not that they do not want to. Jian can see it in the way his mother stands, with her arms folded and her chin up, like a woman at the mouth of a cave who has decided not to look inside. It is in the way Lin Yue has taken his sleeve and will not let go, and in the way Elder Zhong, standing a little apart at the gatehouse door, bows twice instead of once. It is only that the Lin clan has learned, over the last year, that grief is a thing you carry and do not spend.

His father says very little. He has said most of it already, in the forge, in the dark, with a hand on the boy's head. At the gate he only adjusts the strap of Jian's pack, and looks at the knot, and ties it again, tighter, though it was not loose.

"Wenjun has put forty low stones in the left pocket," he says. "Sewn. Do not spend them."

"I will not."

"Two more in the hem. Your mother did those."

"I know."

"The letters go to the Ford, and a rider carries them. It is four days each way." He straightens. His good hand rests for a moment on Jian's shoulder, and the bandaged one hangs at his side. "I will see you at the Register. I will be in the hall. I have been told it is not possible to sit at the back, and I mean to try."

"Father."

"Yes."

"The beds will be well by summer."

"I know," says Wenyuan, quite gently. "You have said."

Qinghe does not say anything at all. She puts both hands on either side of his face, and looks at it for the time it takes to draw one slow breath, as if she were setting it in a drawer. Then she kisses his forehead, hard, once, and lets go.

Lin Yue is the last. She hangs on his sleeve until Zhong gently peels her fingers loose, one by one, and carries her back a step. She does not cry either. She holds up a single finger, and mouths a word: one.

One number, he thinks. How many were nice to you.

He nods.

Behind him, across the yard, a sound has begun in the granary forge. It is a long, clear, level note, a hammer on iron, and then another, and then a third, in the old slow rhythm: down, turn, down. It carries through the cold morning air like a bell. It does not stop when the gate opens. It does not stop when the cart passes through. It is still going when they reach the bend in the road, and Jian turns his head, and sees the pine woods close over the hill like water.

He is not coming to the gate, he thinks. He is saying it the only way he can.

Pebble is in his sleeve, a warm weight against his wrist. She says nothing. After a while, her small claws close on the cloth, and hold.

* * *

The Court has sent one man.

Cheng Yun rides on the box of the cart, beside a hired driver, with a gray cloak over his short robe and his tally-board across his knees. He is thirty-nine now, early Foundation or a little more, lean and weathered, a man who has walked a great many roads on someone else's errand. He has not said ten words since the gate. It is not rudeness. It is the silence of a man who has learned that people say a great deal more when he is not asking.

They reach Willow Ford at midday.

The market is in full cry. It spreads along the river road for half a mile, a long, loud, many-colored crush of stalls and carts and kneeling men, hung with strings of dried peppers and bolts of cloth and cages of green-and-yellow birds. Jian has been here before. He has come in summers, with ingots in a cart, a small gray boy who did not speak. He knows its smells: brine, wet wool, frying dough, the thin sharp sweetness of crushed herbs. He knows its dangers. He moves through it with his hood up and his Seasons Veil turning, shallow and slow.

"Ten minutes," says Cheng Yun, from behind him. "Whatever it is you came for. I will wait by the ferry."

He does not ask what it is. He only sets his tally-board on the cart seat, and strolls off through the crowd with his hands behind his back, to look at the river.

He knows, thinks Jian. He does not care to be told.

The beast shops are at the far end of the market, where the smell of animal will not trouble the jade stalls. A row of low sheds with painted signs. A pen of young hill goats. A tall thin man in a stained apron, selling a pair of three-eyed hares with a loud patience that suggests he has been doing so for a week.

The shop at the end has no sign, only a hide stretched over a hoop, with a ring of stitching in the center like an eye. A woman sits beneath it on an upturned crate, cracking nuts. She is fifty, stout, and entirely without hurry.

"A bag," says Jian.

"For what?"

"A small beast. Not a hunter. A companion."

"What kind?"

He has turned over every lie all winter. "A hatchling," he says. "Sleeps a lot. First rank."

The woman looks at his plain gray cloak, and his clean boots, and the Seasons Veil turning over a boy of no importance. She cracks a nut with her thumb.

"Sixty," she says.

"It is a Yellow-low bag."

"It is a bag." She nods at a row of pouches on the shelf behind her, each the size of a fist, in soft dun leather with a ring of stitched sinew round the mouth. "Real beast hide. Real sinew. Holds one small creature, up to the first rank, in a closed pocket of air with a bed of moss and a little of the beast's own scent, so it does not panic. It does not suffocate. It does not freeze. You may keep it in there a month if it is calm." She spits a shell into the dust. "A month. After that it goes mad."

"Forty," says Jian.

"I said sixty."

"I heard." He picks up a pouch and turns it over. The stitching is even. The sinew is fresh. He puts a finger to the ring at the mouth, and feels, faintly, a small cool breath of something that is not air. It is better made than he expected. "It is a Yellow-low. There is a patch on the seam, here, where the hide has been mended. You have not told me. A good beast bag does not mend."

The woman's cracking hand stops.

"And it has no sleeping rune." He turns it again. "A sleeping rune doubles the price, and I would pay it, if it were there. It is not."

She looks at him a long moment. Something in her face moves, behind the stoutness and the nutshells, and for a moment she is not a stall-woman at all, but a person who has been doing this for thirty years and has met, perhaps twice, a customer who knew what he was looking at.

"Where did you learn to read a bag?" she says.

"From a very good liar." It is not even a lie. "Forty."

"Fifty."

"Forty-five, and you tell me what to put in it so it does not know it is shut."

She laughs. It is a short, harsh, delighted bark. She cracks the last of her nut, and eats it, and wipes her hands on her apron.

"Moss," she says. "From where the beast lives. A handful, damp. And your own sleeve, or a scrap of it, so it smells you. If it can smell you, it will think you are near." She holds out her palm. "Forty-five."

He counts out the stones. Forty-five low stones, from the purse Hu left on his cot the night before, with a note that said only For the bag, is most of what the purse held. He feels every one of them go. He ties the bag to his belt, under the cloak, where it hangs against his hip like a purse of stolen bread.

Against his wrist, very faintly, Pebble gives a long, slow, careful sniff.

It smells, she says, like somewhere that is not a door.

That is all it has to be.

Hm, she says. I will see.

* * *

The road goes north from the Ford for four days.

It is called the Cloud Road, though it has never been near a cloud: a long, pale, dusty ribbon of packed earth, running between wheat-fields and willow groves and the occasional blackened shell of a roadside inn. It was built, the driver says, when the Sect was young, to carry grain and medicines from the lowland clans up to the mountains. Now it carries tribute carts and wandering peddlers and the families of every child who will be Measured this spring.

Jian has watched them pass all morning: a farmer's boy on a mule, two sisters in matching blue, a thin pale girl in a carrying-chair with a tutor on either side. Their eyes are fixed on the horizon, as a man's eyes are fixed on a door he expects to open.

"They come from all the south," says Cheng Yun. He has dropped back on the seat, beside the boy, and is watching the road with his hands folded. "Every affiliated clan sends what it has. A hundred children in a good year. Three hundred in a great one. The Register is the one door the Sect leaves open, and it is not a wide one."

"How many pass?"

"Of three hundred?" He considers. "Forty, to the Outer Court. A dozen to the Gate Hall as servants. The rest go home." He glances at Jian. "You were registered by letter, which is rare. I have seen it twice in nineteen years."

"Yes."

"The first became a Deacon, with a little courtyard and a small, good life." A pause. "The second was a girl. She died."

Jian does not say anything.

"I tell you this," says Cheng Yun, "not to frighten you. I tell you because no one will tell you in the Court itself. Some of the roads go up." He turns his eyes forward. "Most go in circles."

They stop at midday on the second day, at a wayside well under a willow, to water the mule. Cheng Yun climbs down, and stretches, and walks a little way along the bank with his hands behind his back. He stands there for a time, looking at nothing.

When he speaks, he does not turn round.

"The Garden's yield has dropped nine percent," he says. "Since the autumn."

Jian goes quite still.

"The Garden Office noticed it in the first quarter. It is a small fall. Dou thought nothing of it, and wrote cause unknown in the margin, in the Patriarch's own hand, as an honest man does when he has no better answer." He pauses. "I read the margin. It is a very good margin. It is the margin of a man who knows the cause, and has chosen not to put it in a ledger."

The wind moves in the willow. A bird, somewhere, is singing a thin repeating note.

"I am not asking," says Cheng Yun.

"No."

"I have been an inspector for nineteen years. In that time I have learned that the things worth knowing are rarely the things people tell you. I have also learned that a man who hides a thing for a good reason will hide it better than any Court can find it." He turns, at last, and looks at the boy. His eyes are quiet, tired, and entirely level. "I mention it only so that you know it has been noticed. The Arbiter has not read it. I have not filed it. I do not intend to, unless I am required to."

"Why?"

"Because I audited your clan for three days," says Cheng Yun, "and I did not find a single false figure. And because there is a boy in the Outer Court named Lin Feng who limps, and who has never once asked me for anything." A very small pause. "I like to think I am a man who can be told when he is not needed."

He walks back to the cart. He climbs up on the box. He picks up the tally-board and sets it across his knees, as if nothing at all had been said.

Jian stands by the well, with a bucket in his hand and his heart going very fast.

A friend, he thinks. Or a man who thinks he is one.

He does not know which. It is, he supposes, the same kind of thing.

* * *

The ford is on the afternoon of the third day.

It is not Willow Ford. It is a smaller one, a day beyond, where the Cloud Road crosses a shallow, fast, stony river called the Gray Thread on its way down from the hills. There is a wooden ferry, a hut with a sleeping ferryman, and a long line of flat black stepping-stones running from one bank to the other.

Jian sees it, and his skin goes cold.

Too perfect, he thinks.

He studied the map of the Cloud Road in the Lin study a dozen times, tracing it with his finger. There are eleven places along it where a party might be stopped by anything less than an army. The Gray Thread is the best of them. It has water on two sides, a hut for cover, a long open crossing where a cart must slow to a crawl, and a stand of willow on the far bank thick enough to hide a regiment.

If I were Blood Shadow, he thinks, I would be here.

"I will ride ahead," says Cheng Yun, from the box. He has been looking at the same ford, with the same expression, though he says nothing of it. "The ferryman is asleep. I will wake him, and arrange the crossing. It will take a quarter hour. Keep the cart on this bank."

"I will water the mule," says Jian.

"Do." Cheng Yun swings down, and strides toward the hut with his cloak flapping.

Jian does not water the mule.

He takes the leather belt from his waist, the plain, scuffed, nine-loop belt that Hu made him in the summer, and he unrolls it on the gravel bank. There are nine pins in it. Each is the length of a finger, made of gray-blue iron, with a hollow shaft and a little cap of beeswax. He takes six. He pulls up his sleeves. He walks, quietly, to the edge of the water.

He sets the pins into the cracks between the stepping-stones, along the near half of the crossing, two to a stone, in a pattern that is not a pattern, each a hand's breadth from the next. He does not look round. He does not hurry. He tucks a small handful of white river pebbles into the gaps beside each, packing them with his thumb.

Pin snare, he thinks. Six-point. A man steps on the wrong stone, and the pins go through his foot.

He has set the fifth when he feels the Hollow Echo hum.

It is not a sound. It is a feeling, a faint thin pulse in the bone behind his ear. The technique is not one he has called; it is one that has noticed. Somewhere in the willows on the far bank, in the long green dark, something is hollow. Something has been set into the ground there, the size of a man's head, round, and full of liquid, with a wax seal.

Jars, he thinks. Blood jars. Four of them.

Four, says Pebble, from his sleeve, very quiet. And three people. And one who is a little bit louder than the others.

How far?

Forty steps. Not moving.

He does not look at the willows. He sets the sixth pin, with fingers that do not tremble, and rolls the belt closed, and stands. Then, slowly, as if he had thought of nothing at all, he walks back up the bank to the cart, and puts his hand on the mule's neck.

Cheng Yun is at the hut, he thinks. Two hundred paces. He will take a quarter hour. If they know he is gone, they will move in less.

They know.

Of course they do.

The sound comes, when it comes, like a knife drawn in a quiet room.

* * *

The first man comes out of the willows at a dead run.

He is big and fast, in a ragged gray cloak, with a short curved blade in each hand and the thin black thread of a Blood Shadow mark running up one side of his throat. A Drip, fifth stage. He takes the ford at a dash, three steps onto the first stone, four onto the second, with his teeth bared. On the fifth stone, his foot lands on a patch of wet black rock that is exactly the color of the stone beside it, and the beeswax cap beneath his heel cracks, and a thin iron pin, driven by a coil of wire, goes through the arch of his foot and into the rock.

He screams.

The second man is already on the gravel. The third is at the water's edge, pouring something from a jar. Jian does not stop to count them. He has dropped, flat, behind the cart's near wheel, and he is already breathing the long slow breath that brings the Seal round to its summer face. A thread of cold goes up his arm. A second, thicker, heavier one, follows it.

Hollow Echo, he thinks.

He lays two fingers against the wheel's iron rim and lets the pulse go out, not toward the men, but across the water, to the willows, where four small round shapes sit in the dark.

The sound is a long, thin, shivering tink.

Four jars crack.

It is not loud. It is the sound of a bowl, set down too hard on a stone floor. But from the willow thicket on the far bank, a great soft whump rolls up, and a pillar of dull red mist climbs into the air, rank with the stink of rotted iron, rolling and boiling and spreading as it rises. A man cries out. A second answers. The mist drifts, slow and heavy, across the river on the wind, and it does not drift toward the cart.

They carried the fog with them, he thinks, coldly. For the cart. For us.

His head feels as if it has been struck with a mallet. A tenth of his reserve has gone into the recoil, down into the dantian in a single sharp stab. He tastes copper. He grits his teeth and does not let it show.

Eleven.

The man with the broken foot is down on the stones, clawing at the pin. The second, a lean, quick woman with a hooked knife, has leapt the first stone and is racing the gravel bar. The third has dropped his jar, and is backing away, mouth open, from the spreading cloud.

Jian rises.

He does not run at them. He has never been good at that. He walks out from behind the cart, straight toward the water's edge, and the woman with the knife swerves at the sight of him, mouth curling. She is fast. She is very fast. She crosses the last three stones in the time it takes him to draw a breath.

Stone, he thinks. Fourth from the bank. Wet.

She lands on it. It rocks.

It is not a trick of the iron. It is only a rock. He had set a river pebble beneath it, packed with a thumb, so that its far edge stood a finger's width proud of the gravel, and any weight that struck it from the wrong angle would pitch. She pitches. She throws out a hand, and the knife catches the water, and her ankle turns, and in the instant before she can recover he has taken the two steps between them and put the flat of his palm against her breastbone.

Seam Needle.

He lets half of it leak, as he has practiced. A thread of cold, no wider than a hair, goes in under her ribs, at the place Pebble taught him, and stops.

She does not scream. She folds, slowly, and sits down in the river, and stares at him with astonished eyes. Then the black thread at her throat flickers once, and goes out.

One, he thinks. Two.

The man in the water is shouting, hoarse and wild, a name Jian does not catch. The third is running. Not toward the cart: toward the trees. It is the one who has been louder than the others, a small gaunt man with a sallow face and a mark like a spider on the back of his neck. He is not running in fear. He is running as a man runs who has been told to retreat, and who knows where.

Jian lifts his hand.

The man is thirty paces off, hip-deep in the shallows, a dark shape in the red haze. A QR9, at the peak, a layer deeper than any of the others. If he reaches the willows, he is gone.

Hollow Echo, he thinks. Again. And aim.

It is an expensive thought. His reserve is already falling. He has the Seal, and a thousand breaths of control, and the tail of a half-formed idea. He does not throw the pulse at the man. He throws it at the water, a handspan in front of his knees, where the river runs over a pocket of trapped air under a ledge of stone.

The ledge cracks.

It is the smallest thing: a flat black slab, undermined by a hundred years of flow, giving way under a hollow note. But the water above it drops a foot in a single heartbeat, and the man, hip-deep and running, loses his footing and pitches forward into the current. He comes up spluttering. He is on one knee. And in the half-breath before he can rise, Jian has taken from the belt at his waist the last three pins, and thrown them.

They are not a technique. They are only pins. But they are very good pins, and the man is very close, and he is looking in the wrong direction.

One goes through his sleeve. One through the cloak at his shoulder. The third, thrown a little wild, catches the cord of the jar he has slung across his back, and the glass shatters, and the fog that has been waiting in it boils out around his head.

He goes down on both knees, in the shallows, clawing at his own face.

It is quiet then.

Jian stands at the edge of the ford with his hands hanging at his sides, and his heart going like a hammer, and the red fog drifting away down the river like a stain. He is bleeding from the nose again. His hands are shaking. In the water, a man is dying, slowly, in a cloud of his own making, and a woman sits with her eyes open, and on the fifth stone from the bank, a young man with a pin through his foot has stopped screaming and is staring at the sky.

Three, he thinks. And the one with the foot.

There is the sound of boots on gravel.

He does not turn. He knows the step, even and a little too light, the sign of a body rebuilt from the bones. He stands where he is, and watches the river carry the red away.

"I told you to keep the cart on this bank," says Cheng Yun.

He is standing ten paces behind. He has come at a run, and is not out of breath. He has a long sword in his right hand, bare, and his left hand is empty, held a little out from his side, in the way a man holds it who has been about to cast. He is looking at the stones, and the pins, and the packed river pebbles, and the woman in the water. At the ledge, where the stream still runs a little lower than it should.

At the boy.

For a very long moment, he says nothing at all.

"Three Drips," he says at last, slowly, "and a fourth at the peak of the ninth stage. Fog jars of the Blood Shadow's own make, which they carried through the woods for four days to use on a cart that had, as far as they knew, one child and one inspector in it." His eyes do not leave Jian's face. "And you were on the gravel bank, watering a mule."

"Yes."

"With six pins set in the stones. In a pattern that I would have taken, from a distance, for a boy's idle game."

"Yes."

"With a Veil," says Cheng Yun, very quietly, "on a Qi that I read, three days ago, as the third layer of Qi Refining."

Jian does not answer.

"I am not going to ask," says the inspector. He sheathes the sword. It makes a small clean sound. "I said that, and I mean it. But I would like you to understand what I have seen." His voice is level and tired and quite without anger. "I have seen a nineteen-year-old stop four Blood Shadow hunters on a river crossing, without a spell I could name, without a talisman, without a blade. I have seen him do it in less than a minute, with his hands shaking." A pause. "I have been an inspector for nineteen years. I have never in my life seen the Seal do what yours has just done. And I have seen the Seal."

"It is a Yellow technique," says Jian. "A small one."

"It is not."

"It is a thing my mother taught me."

"It is not," says Cheng Yun again, "and you know it is not, and I know. And I would very much like it if neither of us said so in front of anyone at the Court." He crosses the gravel. He stands beside Jian, a head taller, and looks at the river, where the red mist has thinned to nothing. "There is a rule in the Sect. The first Register is a thing that every child is permitted to do alone. No elder may interfere. No elder may ask. It is a kindness, and also a cruelty. I am going to follow it. I will be at the Hall, as a witness. I will not lift a finger."

"Thank you."

"Do not thank me." For the first time, a flicker of something crosses his face, dry and rueful. "It is only that I am not certain, any longer, who is protecting whom."

He turns, and walks back toward the cart.

Jian stays where he is for a little while, by the water. The bleeding has stopped. The Echo's recoil is a dull, heavy pulse behind his eyes, and his reserve, he thinks, is a little over a third. He puts out his hand, and Pebble climbs out of his sleeve, and settles on his shoulder with her claws very lightly pricking the cloth.

They were not here for me, she says.

What?

They were looking for something. A slow, thoughtful pause. One of them, the quiet one. He kept turning his head. Not toward you. Toward your belt.

He glances down.

At his waist, beneath the cloak, wrapped in oiled silk, a plain curved blade lies against his hip. He has carried it for three days. He has not drawn it. He has told no one.

They did not know the hill was empty, he thinks. They did not know what I was carrying. They only knew that something was.

Yes.

The wind stirs in the willows. Somewhere upriver, a bird is singing.

They cross at dusk, on the ferry, in the long red light, and reach the far bank as the first lamps are lit. The road climbs from the water. It climbs through a stand of birch and a long low pass of stone, and as the cart tops the last rise, with the mule blowing and the driver cursing under his breath, Jian lifts his head.

The mountain stands against the sky.

It is not a single mountain. It is a wall of them, a great ragged line of peaks fading from violet to blue to the pale white of snow, and on the nearest, running up its flank in a long unbroken thread, a staircase of fire. Hundreds of steps. Thousands. Each lit by a small, steady, golden lamp, climbing from the valley floor to a gate at the very top, where the Sect's banners hang in the last of the light.

And a little below the gate, set apart from the rest, a single stretch of forty steps burns brighter than all the others, a hard cold white, as if something at the end of them were looking back.
